progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: First video of this series: asexual reproduction is one parent making a copy without gametes joining, offspring are clones apart from rare copying errors, and fast copying suits steady conditions. Cells contain DNA, and some cells have a nucleus (given a one-clause meaning in scene 4). Powers of two.
progression.startsWith: A glass of milk on a warm bench that turns sour, and the single bacterium it started from.
progression.stopsAfter: Describing binary fission and budding as copy, share, split with a bacterium, baker's yeast, an amoeba, a paramecium and a budding protist; explaining why DNA is copied before the cell splits; working out a doubling time example; and separating conjugation (DNA moved, no split, no new cell) from reproduction.
progression.nextLesson: B3a: what happens after a mammal's egg is fertilised (implantation, pregnancy and hormones).

teaching.task: Explain how a single-celled organism makes a new cell, work out how many cells a doubling population reaches, and decide whether conjugation is reproduction.
teaching.causalExplanation: A cell that simply pinched in half would leave one half with no DNA and no instructions, so the DNA is copied first, the copies are shared, then the cell splits. Fission turns the parent into two new cells and budding grows a new cell from a parent that carries on. Each doubling multiplies the whole crowd by two, so n doublings gives 2 to the power n cells until food runs out or waste builds up. Conjugation passes DNA between two existing cells without a split, so the number of cells does not change and it is not reproduction.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens with sour milk and one bacterium with no partner, asks what goes wrong if a cell just pinches in half, builds one pattern (copy, share, split) across a bacterium, yeast, amoeba, paramecium and Acineta, works the doubling calculation one stage at a time, and separates conjugation with a count of cells before and after.
teaching.openingDecision: A bacterium has no partner to join with. How does one cell make another cell, and how does that become a crowd?
teaching.understandingCheck: Say which step failed when one new cell has one DNA loop and the other none, decide whether a bridge passing a gene between two bacteria is reproduction and what changed and what stayed the same, and work out the cells after 2 hours for a 40 minute doubling time.
teaching.curriculumScope: Describe asexual reproduction in single-celled organisms: binary fission and budding, with conjugation separated from reproduction (Module 5). Mitosis stages, spores and mould, and sexual protist life cycles are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, B1 fission and budding plates reused with new aligned amoeba plates and single painted milk glass, paramecium and Acineta plates, a coded numbered copy, share, split strip, a doubling grid and a coded conjugation bridge.
design.transitionPlan: The magnifier pushes from the milk glass to one bacterium; fission plates crossfade in order with the strip as a rail; the board clears for the doubling example; the budding plates replace the bacterium; a pond-water field replaces the bench for the protists; the conjugation drawing reuses the bacterium art; the three-column board assembles one column at a time; scene crossfade with settle.
